client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died last year — it was a car accident, and it just kind of knocked the ground out from under me. Everything that used to feel normal, like going out with friends or even just watching a movie, feels hollow now, like I'm just going through the motions. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: What you've been carrying since losing your brother sounds truly devastating — grief like this can strip the color right out of life, leaving even the things you once loved feeling distant and empty. I'm really glad you decided to try something, and I want you to know that just showing up here, even with doubt, takes real courage. Can you tell me a little more about what a typical day looks like for you right now — what it feels like from the inside when you're "going through the motions"?

client: A typical day is just... flat, I guess. I wake up and there's this immediate heaviness, like my body already knows before I'm even fully conscious that something's wrong, and then I remember, and it's like losing him all over again for a second. I go to work, I talk to people, I even laugh sometimes, but it all feels like I'm watching myself from a distance, like I'm not really there.
therapist: That experience of watching yourself from a distance — like you're behind glass from your own life — is something many people feel in deep grief, and it makes a lot of sense given the weight you wake up carrying every single day. What strikes me is that even through all of that flatness, you *are* still showing up — to work, to people — and I'm curious what that costs you. When you're laughing or talking with someone and it feels hollow, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, the thought that comes up most is something like "you shouldn't be laughing right now" — like there's this internal monitor that catches me whenever I start to feel anything close to normal and reminds me that my brother is dead and I have no right to enjoy anything. And then I feel guilty on top of everything else, which just makes the whole thing worse. It's exhausting, like I'm punishing myself for still being alive while he isn't.
therapist: That inner monitor sounds absolutely exhausting — like a part of you has appointed itself to make sure you never get too far from the pain, almost as if enjoying something feels like a betrayal of your brother. This is something we call survivor's guilt, and it's incredibly common in grief, but that doesn't make it any less cruel to live with. I want to gently ask — do you think your brother would have wanted you to sentence yourself to a life without joy or laughter?

client: I know what you're going for with that question, and logically I can tell myself "no, he'd want me to be happy" — he was that kind of person, genuinely. But it doesn't actually make the guilt go away when I feel it in the moment, it just adds another layer where I feel guilty for still feeling guilty, if that makes sense. Like knowing something in your head and actually feeling it in your gut are two completely different things.
therapist: You're naming something really important — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is one of the most frustrating parts of grief, and honestly, you're right that insight alone rarely closes it. In CBT we actually work with that gap directly, not by trying to think your way out of the feeling, but by slowly building small experiences that can start to shift what your gut believes over time. I'm wondering — when that inner monitor shows up in the moment and says "you have no right to feel this," what does it feel like you'd be losing if you didn't listen to it?

client: That's a question I haven't really thought about before, and it's making me uncomfortable in a way I can't quite explain. I think... if I stopped listening to it, it would feel like I was letting him go, like the guilt is the last thing keeping me connected to him, keeping him real. Which sounds messed up when I say it out loud, but maybe the pain is the only place he still exists for me right now.
therapist: What you just said doesn't sound messed up at all — it sounds like one of the most honest and tender things a person can say about grief, and it takes real courage to see that in yourself. That connection between pain and love makes complete sense: when someone is gone, the grief can feel like the only thread still holding you to them. I want to sit with that for a moment, and then gently ask — do you think there might be other ways of staying connected to your brother, ways that carry him forward with you, that don't require you to punish yourself to keep him real?

client: Maybe, but I honestly don't know what that would even look like — like, the idea sounds nice in theory, but when I try to picture it, I just draw a blank. We used to do things together, watch certain shows, go to this one diner, but now those things just feel like reminders of what's gone rather than ways to keep him close. I'm not sure I'm ready to turn them into something that feels okay yet.
therapist: The quiet honesty in what you're sharing — that you're just not ready yet — is really important, and it deserves to be respected rather than rushed. Grief has its own timeline, and there's a real difference between forcing yourself to "make peace" with those places and shows before you're ready, and simply leaving the door open for a day when they might feel like more than just loss. I'm wondering, when you think about your brother, is there anything — even something small — that brings up a feeling closer to warmth or gratitude rather than just pain?

client: There's this one thing — he used to send me these completely ridiculous memes at like two in the morning, the dumbest stuff, and sometimes when I think about that specifically I feel something that's almost like a smile before the sadness crashes in. It's such a small, stupid thing, but it was so him. I don't know, even saying that out loud right now feels like a tiny crack of light, but then I immediately feel guilty for it, like I'm back in that same loop again.
therapist: That tiny crack of light you just described — that almost-smile before the sadness rushes in — that *is* him, still reaching you, still being exactly who he was. And notice what just happened: you held something warm about your brother, even for a moment, without it erasing him or meaning you've let him go. I wonder if that little crack of light might actually be one of the truest ways he still exists for you — not in the guilt, but in the ridiculous two-in-the-morning dumbness that was so completely, specifically him?

client: That actually landed differently than I expected, and I'm sitting here feeling a little caught off guard by it. Like, I hadn't thought about it that way — that the memes are more him than the guilt is, because the guilt is mine, but those ridiculous pictures were actually his personality. I'm not ready to say the guilt is just something I should drop, but that's... a different way of seeing it that I want to think about.
therapist: What you just did — making that distinction between the guilt being *yours* and the memes being *his* — is genuinely meaningful work, and the fact that it caught you off guard tells me it touched something real. You don't have to be ready to drop the guilt; just holding that new perspective gently, without forcing it, is exactly the right pace. As you sit with it this week, I'm curious — when that almost-smile shows up before the sadness crashes in, do you think you might be able to let it stay just a breath longer, and notice what that feels like?

client: I want to say yes, but I'm also a little scared that if I let that feeling stay longer, the guilt will just hit harder afterward, like I'm setting myself up for a bigger crash. It's like I've learned to keep those moments short as a kind of self-protection, so deliberately stretching them out feels risky in a way I can't fully explain. I'll try, but I'm not making any promises.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you've developed that self-protection for a real reason, and it's actually been doing a job for you, even if it's a costly one. "I'll try, but no promises" is honestly the perfect answer — this isn't about forcing yourself into anything, just maybe getting a little curious about what happens rather than committing to a outcome. And if the guilt does crash in harder sometimes, that's something we can work with together rather than something you have to brace against alone.

client: That last part you said — that I don't have to brace against it alone — actually got to me a little, because I think that's been a big part of what makes this so hard. Since he died, I've felt like I have to manage all of this by myself, like I can't really show people how bad it is because then they'd worry or not know what to say and it would just get awkward. I'm not used to the idea that someone could actually be there when it gets worse instead of it just being my problem to contain.
therapist: What you're describing — carrying all of this quietly so others don't have to feel uncomfortable — is such a lonely way to grieve, and it makes the weight so much heavier than it needs to be. There's something really significant in the fact that you let that land just now, that you let yourself feel the possibility of not being alone in it, even just for a moment. I want to gently ask — is there anyone in your life, even one person, who you think might actually be able to show up for you if you let them see a little more of what this has really been like?
